miguel-hidalgo#summary: The father of the Mexican nation, whose Cry of Dolores in 1810 set off the struggle for independence.
miguel-hidalgo#text: Hidalgo, the son of an estate manager, was an educated priest who read Rousseau, promoted workshops and viticulture in his parish of Dolores and spoke with indigenous farmers in their own language. When a conspiracy against Spanish rule was betrayed, he rang the church bells on 16 September 1810 and called for an uprising; under the banner of the Virgin of Guadalupe an army of as many as 80,000 people followed him, took the city of Guanajuato and committed massacres of Spaniards. Before Mexico City he hesitated, was defeated near Guadalajara in January 1811, captured while fleeing north, stripped of his office by the church and shot in Chihuahua on 30 July 1811. His call for the abolition of slavery and of tribute made him Mexico's national hero.
freiherr-vom-stein#name: Heinrich Friedrich Karl vom und zum Stein
freiherr-vom-stein#summary: The imperial baron who launched the Prussian reforms in 1807 and became Napoleon's most implacable opponent in Germany.
freiherr-vom-stein#text: Stein came from a family of imperial knights in Nassau and served Prussia from 1780 as an administrative official and finally as minister; because of his criticism of the cabinet system he was dismissed in January 1807. After the defeat at Tilsit the king recalled him in October 1807, and within a year Stein pushed through the emancipation of the peasants, the municipal ordinance and a reorganization of the ministries in order to involve citizens in administration. When an intercepted letter revealed his hope for an uprising against France, Napoleon forced his dismissal at the end of 1808 and outlawed him; Stein fled to Austria and in 1812 to Russia, where he urged Tsar Alexander to war against Napoleon. In 1813 he organized the administration of the liberated territories, called in vain for a German nation-state and in 1819 founded the Monumenta Germaniae Historica for the study of the Middle Ages.
mary-wollstonecraft#role: English writer and pioneer of women's rights
mary-wollstonecraft#summary: The author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, who in 1792 demanded equal education and civil rights for women.
mary-wollstonecraft#text: Wollstonecraft grew up in an impoverished family with a violent father, worked as a companion, teacher and governess, and from 1787 made her way in London as a translator and author, which was unusual for a woman of her time. In response to the French Revolution and to Rousseau's view that women were destined to be educated to please men, she published A Vindication of the Rights of Woman in 1792: women appeared weaker and more superficial only because education was withheld from them; she called for coeducational schools, professions of their own and political representation. From 1792 to 1795 she experienced the Reign of Terror in Paris, had a daughter out of wedlock and described her journey to Scandinavia. She died in 1797 a few days after the birth of her daughter Mary, the later author of Frankenstein. In the 19th century her work became a foundation of the women's movement.
spartacus#role: Gladiator and leader of a slave revolt
spartacus#summary: The Thracian gladiator who led the largest slave revolt of antiquity from 73 to 71 BC.
spartacus#text: Spartacus came from Thrace in present-day Bulgaria, probably served in Roman auxiliary troops and was sold as a prisoner to the gladiator school at Capua. In 73 BC he escaped with about 70 companions and led a rapidly growing army of slaves and farm laborers that defeated several Roman armies; the sources praise his shrewdness and his fairness in distributing plunder. His aim of crossing the Alps and releasing the slaves to their homelands foundered on his followers' wish to go on plundering Italy. In 71 BC he fell in battle against Crassus; his body was never found. Since the 18th century he has been a symbol of the struggle for freedom.
kleopatra-vii#summary: The last ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt, who allied herself with Caesar and Antony and with whose death her country fell to Rome.
kleopatra-vii#text: Cleopatra came to the throne at 18 and held her own against her brother and co-ruler by winning Caesar to her side in 48 BC; their son Caesarion was to secure the dynasty. She was highly educated, the first Ptolemy to speak Egyptian along with eight other languages, and ruled a rich but Rome-dependent country. After Caesar's death she allied herself with Mark Antony, to whom she bore three children, and shared rule over the East with him. After the defeat at Actium and Octavian's entry into Alexandria she took her own life in 30 BC, by legend through the bite of a snake; Egypt became a Roman province.
livia#summary: Wife of Augustus and mother of Tiberius, who for more than five decades was the most powerful woman in Rome.
livia#text: Livia married Octavian in 38 BC, who took her from her first husband although she was pregnant. In 52 years of marriage she became the closest adviser of Augustus, received envoys, managed a great fortune with estates and brickworks of her own, and was regarded as the model of the virtuous Roman matron who wove the emperor's clothing herself. At the same time she secured the succession for Tiberius, her son from her first marriage; rumors that she poisoned rivals are unproven but shaped her image down to Robert Graves's novel I, Claudius. Augustus adopted her in his will as Julia Augusta; her grandson Claudius had her raised to the status of a goddess in 42.
nero#summary: The last emperor of the house of Augustus, notorious for matricide, the fire of Rome and the first persecution of Christians.
nero#text: Nero became emperor in 54 at the age of 16, after his mother Agrippina had probably poisoned the emperor Claudius. Guided by the philosopher Seneca he governed moderately at first, but then had his mother killed in 59 and his wife Octavia in 62. During the great fire of Rome in 64, which devastated ten of the fourteen districts, he was accused of arson; he directed suspicion onto the Christians and had them cruelly executed, and on the ruins he built his enormous palace, the Domus Aurea. Nero performed as a singer, poet and charioteer and toured Greece, which outraged the senators. When governors and praetorians rose against him he took his own life in 68 with the words what an artist dies in me; the Year of the Four Emperors followed.
trajan#summary: The best emperor in the judgment of the Senate, under whom the empire reached its greatest extent.
trajan#text: Trajan was born in Italica near Seville in Spain, the first emperor from a province, and was adopted in 97 by the aged Nerva. As a commander he conquered Dacia and campaigned against the Parthians as far as the Persian Gulf. In Rome he used the spoils to build the Forum of Trajan with markets, libraries and Trajan's Column, built harbors, roads and aqueducts in the provinces and created with the alimenta a fund to support poor children in Italy. His correspondence with the governor Pliny shows how he attended to details of administration and did not have Christians actively persecuted. The Senate gave him the title Optimus Princeps, best of rulers; centuries later new emperors were still wished to be luckier than Augustus and better than Trajan.
marc-aurel#summary: The philosopher on the imperial throne, who fought Germanic peoples on the Danube and wrote his Meditations.
marc-aurel#text: Marcus Aurelius was adopted by the emperor Antoninus Pius and succeeded him on the throne in 161, at first jointly with Lucius Verus. His reign was marked by crises: a war against the Parthians, a plague carried in from the East that killed millions, and from 166 invasions by the Marcomanni and Quadi that reached northern Italy forced him to spend years in camp on the Danube. There he wrote the Meditations in Greek, notes of a Stoic on duty, transience and composure, which are among the most widely read books of antiquity. He died in 180 at Vindobona, today's Vienna, or at Sirmium; with his son Commodus the age of the adoptive emperors ended. His equestrian statue on the Capitol is the only surviving one of a Roman emperor.
hypatia#summary: The most famous scholar of late antiquity, who taught in Alexandria and was murdered by a Christian mob.
hypatia#text: Hypatia was the daughter of the mathematician Theon, the last known scholar of the Museion of Alexandria, and in the judgment of her contemporaries she surpassed her father. She wrote commentaries on the works of Diophantus and Apollonius and on the tables of Ptolemy, built astrolabes and, as head of a Neoplatonic school, taught philosophy to pagans and Christians alike; her student Synesius became a bishop. As an adviser to the city prefect Orestes she was drawn into his power struggle with Bishop Cyril. In March 415 a crowd of Christian fanatics dragged her from her carriage, killed her in a church with shards and burned her body. Her death is regarded as a symbol of the end of ancient scholarship and of the conflict between faith and reason.
homo-habilis#summary: The handy human, one of the oldest species of the genus Homo, associated with the first stone tools.
homo-habilis#text: Homo habilis was described in 1964 by Louis Leakey and his colleagues from finds in the Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania; the name means handy human, because the Oldowan tools were attributed to it. It lived about 2.4 to 1.6 million years ago in East Africa, stood only about 1.20 meters tall and had a brain roughly half the size of that of people today, but distinctly larger than that of the australopithecines. Whether it was a direct ancestor of Homo erectus or a side branch is disputed among researchers.
homo-erectus#summary: The first human species with a human-like body, which left Africa, made hand axes and used fire.
homo-erectus#text: Homo erectus, the upright human, arose in Africa just under two million years ago. With long legs, short arms and a height of up to 1.80 meters, it was an enduring walker and hunter. The Turkana Boy from Kenya, an almost complete skeleton from 1.6 million years ago, is its best known fossil. Homo erectus developed the hand axe, mastered fire by at least 400,000 years ago and lived in Africa, Europe and Asia; on Java the last groups survived until about 110,000 years ago. Neanderthals, Denisovans and Homo sapiens probably descend from it.
denisova-mensch#summary: A sister species of the Neanderthals that lived in Asia and was discovered only in 2010 through DNA analysis.
denisova-mensch#text: In 2010, researchers at the Max Planck Institute in Leipzig succeeded in recovering the genome of a previously unknown human species from a tiny finger bone from Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains. The Denisovans were related to the Neanderthals and lived in Siberia, on the Tibetan plateau and probably in Southeast Asia as well. Fossils are rare: a lower jaw from Tibet, a few teeth and bones. Their genetic legacy lives on, however, since people today in New Guinea, Australia and parts of East Asia carry up to five percent Denisovan DNA, including a gene variant that helps Tibetans live at high altitude.
homo-floresiensis#summary: The hobbit of Flores, a human species only about a meter tall on an Indonesian island.
homo-floresiensis#text: In 2003, archaeologists discovered in the Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores the remains of people who were only about 1.06 meters tall and had very small brains. Nevertheless they made stone tools, hunted dwarf elephants and probably used fire. The species lived from at least 100,000 to about 50,000 years ago and disappeared around the time Homo sapiens reached the region. It probably descended from Homo erectus or an even older human form that became smaller on the island through insular dwarfism.
frau-von-pestera-muierii#role: Fossil of an early Homo sapiens in Europe
frau-von-pestera-muierii#summary: A woman's skull about 35,000 years old from Romania, whose genome offers insight into the first modern humans in Europe.
frau-von-pestera-muierii#text: In the cave of Peștera Muierii, the Cave of the Women, near Baia de Fier in Romania, the skull of a woman who lived about 35,000 years ago was found in 1952. She is among the oldest known modern humans in Europe and lived at a time when Neanderthals still inhabited the continent. In 2021 her genome was decoded: it shows high genetic diversity and a Neanderthal component of about three percent. The study proves that the first Europeans were by no means a small, impoverished group, as had long been assumed.
kennewick-mann#role: Skeleton of an early inhabitant of North America
kennewick-mann#summary: A skeleton about 9,000 years old from the US state of Washington, over which a long dispute broke out between science and Indigenous tribes.
kennewick-mann#text: In 1996, an almost complete skeleton of a man who had died about 8,900 years ago at around the age of 40 was found on the bank of the Columbia River near Kennewick. He was about 1.70 meters tall, had a healed spear point in his pelvis and lived on fish and game. Whether he should be studied scientifically or buried according to the wishes of the Indigenous tribes was fought over in court for years. In 2015 a DNA analysis showed that he is closely related to the Indigenous people of the region today; in 2017 the man, called the Ancient One by the tribes, was ceremonially laid to rest.
claus-von-stauffenberg#role: Officer and leading figure of the assassination attempt of 20 July 1944
claus-von-stauffenberg#summary: The severely wounded colonel placed the bomb in Hitler's headquarters and was shot the same night.
claus-von-stauffenberg#text: Stauffenberg came from the Swabian nobility, was shaped by Catholicism and influenced by the poet Stefan George. As a young officer he welcomed parts of National Socialist policy, but the crimes against Jews and civilians in Poland and the Soviet Union and the looming military catastrophe led him to the resistance. In April 1943 an air attack in Tunisia cost him an eye, his right hand and two fingers of his left. As chief of staff to the commander of the reserve army he had access to Hitler's situation briefings from 1944 and took on the assassination himself, even though he also had to lead the coup in Berlin. After it failed he was shot shortly after midnight in the courtyard of the Bendlerblock; his last cry is said to have been for a sacred Germany.
dietrich-bonhoeffer#summary: Opposed National Socialism as a pastor, joined the conspiracy against Hitler and was executed a few weeks before the end of the war.
dietrich-bonhoeffer#text: The son of a Berlin psychiatrist was a lecturer in theology at 24 and in 1933 was among the first to protest publicly against the exclusion of Jews from the church. He became a leading figure of the Confessing Church and directed its illegal preachers' seminary at Finkenwalde until the Gestapo closed it. In 1939 he returned to Germany from the safety of the United States, because he wanted a voice after the war only if he had shared the ordeal with his people. Through his brother-in-law Hans von Dohnanyi he worked for the military intelligence service Abwehr, which served as cover for the resistance, and helped Jews escape to Switzerland. He was arrested in April 1943; in prison he wrote the letters that became famous as Letters and Papers from Prison. After 20 July, material that was found incriminated him severely, and on 9 April 1945 he was hanged in the Flossenbürg concentration camp on Hitler's express order.
oskar-schindler#role: Businessman and rescuer of about 1,200 Jews
oskar-schindler#summary: The Nazi party member and war profiteer saved about 1,200 Jewish forced laborers from murder in his factories in Kraków and Brünnlitz.
oskar-schindler#text: Schindler came from Zwittau in Moravia, joined the Nazi party in 1939 and after the invasion of Poland took over an enamelware factory in Kraków, where he employed Jewish forced laborers because they were cheaper. The businessman became a rescuer: with bribery, alcohol and good connections to the SS he arranged for his workers to be considered indispensable and spared from deportation out of the Płaszów camp of the notorious commandant Amon Göth. When the factory had to be relocated in 1944, he and his wife Emilie compiled a list of about 1,200 names whom he took with him to Brünnlitz in Moravia; there his plant deliberately produced unusable ammunition until the end of the war, and Emilie Schindler cared for sick prisoners. After the war Schindler failed in business in Argentina and Germany and lived on the support of those he had saved. Yad Vashem honored him as Righteous Among the Nations, he was buried in Jerusalem at his own wish, and Steven Spielberg's film Schindler's List made his story known worldwide in 1993.
charles-de-gaulle#role: French general and leader of Free France
charles-de-gaulle#summary: Called from London in 1940 for the fight to continue, led Free France and later founded the Fifth Republic.
charles-de-gaulle#text: The career officer from Lille had argued in vain in the 1930s for a modern armored force and had only just been appointed general and under-secretary of state in June 1940 when the government sought an armistice. He flew to London and on 18 June 1940, in a BBC radio address, called on the French to continue the fight, for France had lost a battle but not the war. From a few thousand volunteers he built the forces of Free France, won the colonies in Africa to his cause and in 1943 united the Resistance inside the country under his leadership. In August 1944 he entered Paris at the head of the liberators and led the provisional government until 1946. In 1958 he returned to power during the Algerian crisis, created the Fifth Republic with a strong president and governed until 1969; he sealed the reconciliation with Germany in 1963 together with Konrad Adenauer.
erwin-rommel#role: Field marshal and commander of the Afrika Korps
erwin-rommel#summary: The Desert Fox, celebrated by Nazi propaganda, was forced to take his own life after 20 July 1944.
erwin-rommel#text: Rommel, a Württemberger, had distinguished himself as a daring officer in the First World War and became a favorite of the dictator through his book Infantry Attacks and as commander of Hitler's escort battalion. In the western campaign of 1940 he drove the 7th Panzer Division forward so quickly that it was called the Ghost Division; from 1941 he commanded the Afrika Korps and captured Tobruk in 1942, for which he was made the youngest field marshal. Goebbels's propaganda turned him into a popular hero, and even the British admired the Desert Fox. After the defeat at El Alamein and the Allied landing in Normandy, whose defense he was to organize, he lost faith in victory and had contact with the conspirators of 20 July without taking part in the attempt himself. When his name came up in interrogations, Hitler gave him the choice in October 1944 between the People's Court and poison; Rommel took his own life and received a state funeral with the lie that he had died of his wounds. Historians today see him in more nuanced terms than the myth of the decent soldier: he was a gifted field commander who served the regime loyally until late.
hirohito#summary: Revered as a divine tenno, he presided over Japan's expansionist policy and himself announced the surrender in 1945.
hirohito#text: Hirohito came to the throne in 1926 and gave his reign the name Showa, enlightened peace. Under the constitution he was supreme commander and a god in human form; in practice he largely left politics to the government and the military, who led Japan into Manchuria in 1931, into China in 1937 and into war against the United States in 1941; his personal responsibility for war decisions and war crimes remains disputed to this day. After the atomic bombs and the Soviet declaration of war he pressed for surrender within a divided leadership and on 15 August 1945 spoke by radio for the first time to his people, who had never heard his voice. The American occupation under General MacArthur refrained from prosecuting him in order to keep Japan stable; in 1946 Hirohito declared that he was not a god and under the new constitution became a symbol of the state without political power. He reigned until his death in 1989 as the longest-serving emperor of Japan and saw the country rise to become an economic power.
alan-turing#summary: Broke the German Enigma cipher at Bletchley Park and laid the theoretical foundations of the computer.
alan-turing#text: In 1936, as a 24-year-old mathematician in Cambridge, Turing described an imagined machine capable of solving any computable task, and with it created the theoretical model of the computer. From 1939 he worked at the British secret center Bletchley Park, where, building on the earlier work of Polish cryptologists, he designed the electromechanical bombe that determined the daily settings of the German Enigma cipher machine. In 1941 his section cracked the radio traffic of the U-boats, which allowed the Allies to route convoys around the German wolf packs; by some estimates the decryption shortened the war by years and saved hundreds of thousands of lives, but it remained secret for decades. After the war Turing designed computing machines and in 1950 formulated the Turing test for artificial intelligence. In 1952 he was convicted for his homosexuality and forced to undergo hormone treatment; in 1954 he died of cyanide poisoning, probably by suicide. The British government apologized in 2009, and in 2013 he was pardoned.
ezana#summary: The king of Aksum under whom the kingdom became Christian in the 4th century.
ezana#text: Ezana ruled the kingdom of Aksum in present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea around the middle of the 4th century. He was educated by the Syrian Christian Frumentius, who later became the first bishop of Aksum. Around 330 Ezana adopted Christianity, as can be seen from the symbol of the cross on his coins. In multilingual stone inscriptions he reported on campaigns against neighboring peoples and as far as Meroe on the Nile. He is venerated as a saint in the Ethiopian church.
koenig-lalibela#role: King of the Zagwe dynasty in Ethiopia
koenig-lalibela#summary: The Ethiopian king to whom tradition attributes the building of the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela.
koenig-lalibela#text: Lalibela ruled Christian Ethiopia in the late 12th and early 13th centuries as king of the Zagwe dynasty. According to tradition, he had eleven churches carved out of the rock in his residence town of Roha, which was later named after him. The complex was meant to represent a new Jerusalem for Ethiopian pilgrims. The Ethiopian church venerates him as a saint. His exact dates are uncertain.
sundiata-keita#summary: The Malinke prince who defeated the Sosso around 1235 and founded the Mali Empire.
sundiata-keita#text: According to tradition, Sundiata Keita was a Malinke prince who was lame as a child and learned to walk only late. After the Sosso king Sumanguru had subjugated his homeland, he united the Mande peoples and won at Kirina around 1235. He became the first ruler of the Mali Empire, which became a great power under his successors. His life is known above all through the epic of Sundiata, which griots still perform today. Historically certain details about him are therefore rare.
sunni-ali#summary: The conqueror who made Songhai a great power on the Niger from 1464.
sunni-ali#text: Sunni Ali ruled Songhai, with its capital Gao, from 1464 to 1492. With cavalry and a fleet of boats on the Niger he conquered Timbuktu in 1468 and later Djenné, creating an empire larger than old Mali. He was officially a Muslim but also relied on the traditional religions of his people. Muslim chroniclers in Timbuktu therefore portrayed him, also because of his harsh treatment of scholars, as a cruel ruler. After his death Askia Mohammed overthrew his son.
askia-mohammed#summary: The ruler under whom Songhai reached its greatest extent and a flowering of Islamic scholarship.
askia-mohammed#text: Mohammed Ture was a general of Sunni Ali and seized power in Songhai in 1493, taking the title askia. He divided the empire into provinces with governors, created a standing army and standardized weights and measures. On his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1496 to 1497 he received from the caliph in Cairo the title of his deputy for the Sudan. He supported the scholars of Timbuktu and Djenné and based his rule on Islam. In 1528, at an advanced age, he was deposed by his son.
afonso-i-von-kongo#summary: The Christian king of Kongo who sought exchange with Portugal while lamenting the consequences of the slave trade.
afonso-i-von-kongo#text: Afonso, whose African name was Mvemba a Nzinga, was a son of King Nzinga a Nkuwu and prevailed in the struggle for the succession in 1509. He made Christianity the state religion, had churches and schools built and sent young nobles to Portugal; his son Henrique was consecrated bishop. In numerous letters to the Portuguese kings he negotiated over trade, missionaries and craftsmen. Particularly well known are his complaints of 1526 about Portuguese traders carrying off free subjects. He reigned for more than three decades and died around 1542.
njinga-von-ndongo#summary: The queen who for decades fought the Portuguese colonial power in present-day Angola through war and diplomacy.
njinga-von-ndongo#text: Njinga was the daughter of a king of Ndongo and appeared in Luanda in 1622 as her brother's envoy, where she negotiated a peace treaty. From 1624 she ruled herself, but had to give way before the Portuguese and conquered the neighboring kingdom of Matamba. At times she allied herself with the Dutch, who occupied Luanda from 1641 to 1648, and took refugees and runaway slaves into her army. In 1656 she made peace with Portugal and ruled until her death in 1663. In present-day Angola she is regarded as a symbol of resistance.
osei-tutu#role: First ruler (asantehene) of the Asante Empire
osei-tutu#summary: The founder of the Asante Empire, who created a lasting symbol of unity in the Golden Stool.
osei-tutu#text: Osei Tutu was ruler of Kumasi and united several Akan states in present-day Ghana into a confederation. Together with the priest Okomfo Anokye he introduced the Golden Stool as the sacred symbol of the realm. Around 1701 he defeated the kingdom of Denkyira at Feyiase and became the first asantehene. He gave the empire laws and a constitution with a council of chiefs. He was killed around 1717 in a war against the Akyem.
usman-dan-fodio#role: Scholar, preacher and founder of the Sokoto Caliphate
usman-dan-fodio#summary: The Fulani scholar whose reform movement led to the founding of the Sokoto Caliphate.
usman-dan-fodio#text: Usman dan Fodio came from a family of Fulani scholars in the Hausa state of Gobir and worked for decades as a teacher and preacher. He criticized unjust taxes, arbitrary rule and the mixing of Islam with older customs. After breaking with the king of Gobir he called for jihad in 1804 and was proclaimed Commander of the Faithful by his followers. He left the administration of the new caliphate largely to his son Muhammad Bello and his brother Abdullahi. He left numerous writings in Arabic and Fulfulde.
nana-asmau#role: Scholar, poet and teacher in the Sokoto Caliphate
nana-asmau#summary: The daughter of Usman dan Fodio, who worked as a poet and organizer of women's education in the Sokoto Caliphate.
